---
# This chapter contains executable marimo cells (see @sec-marimo).
engine: marimo
pyproject: |
  requires-python = "==3.13.*"
  dependencies = [
    "marimo==0.25.2",
    "matplotlib==3.11.2",
    "pandas==3.1.1",
    "tabulate==0.10.0",
  ]
---

# Layout: Typesetting with Quarto {#sec-layout}

This template uses [Quarto](https://quarto.org), an open-source publishing
system. You write your text in *Markdown*, a plain-text format with a very small
set of formatting rules. Quarto converts it with Pandoc into LaTeX and LaTeX
produces the PDF. You thus get the typographic quality of LaTeX, which is
based on TeX, developed by Donald Knuth [@knuth:tex], without having to write
LaTeX yourself. Wherever Markdown is not sufficient, you can still use LaTeX
directly. Some further advantages over conventional word processing are:

Free/platform-independent
: Quarto and LaTeX are free software. No proprietary editor is required; the
  documents can be edited on *any* computer with *any* editor. VS Code,
  Positron and RStudio have Quarto support with a live preview.

Pure text format
: The source text -- the `.qmd` files -- is pure text. This makes the documents
  ideal for version control with git. This in turn enables efficient
  collaboration between you and your supervisor, e.g. via issues and pull
  requests.

Splitting large documents
: Every chapter lives in its own file in the folder `chapters/`. The order of
  the chapters is defined in `_quarto.yml`.

Separating layout/content
: The layout of the entire document is defined once, in the Quarto extension
  in `_extensions/thk-thesis/`. You can concentrate fully on writing.

Professional result
: A document typeset with LaTeX looks more professional than a corresponding
  document created with word processing. This is especially true for math-heavy
  documents, but other documents also benefit from a uniform layout, consistent
  gray value of the continuous text, more consistent page breaks and
  high-quality vector graphics.

Executable
: Python code in [marimo](https://marimo.io) cells runs while rendering and
  inserts the resulting figures and tables. Your evaluation then stays
  reproducible, see @sec-marimo.

The following @sec-hood to @sec-template deal with various aspects that you
should consider when creating your document.

## Under the Hood {#sec-hood}

In your `.qmd` files, you define what your content is (text with structure,
images, tables, references, ...) and how it should roughly look in each case
(e.g. placement of images in *floating environments*, see @sec-figures).

When creating the final document, LaTeX applies a whole host of rules
"under the hood" that determine how everything can be implemented in
the best possible way. These rules concern, for example, the proportion of text
and images per page, spacing within lines, but also special cases such as
avoiding individual lines of a section alone on a page (so-called
"orphans" or "widows").

As a result, for example, your illustrations might "jump" while you are
working on your text. This may well be correct and can be optimized at the end
if necessary.

In this context, avoid interfering with the design process, e.g. by manually
inserting line breaks or spacing. Please only make exceptions in justified
cases.

## Headings {#sec-headings}

In this template, the chapter (`#`) is the highest level of structure. Each
chapter file starts with exactly one of them. This is followed by sections
(`##`) and subsections (`###`). These three levels are numbered and appear in
the table of contents. If you want to structure your text further, there is
also `####`. A heading gets an identifier for cross-references with
`{#sec-name}`, an unnumbered heading with `{.unnumbered}`:

```markdown
# Formal Structure {#sec-formal}

## Sequence {#sec-sequence}

# Abstract {.unnumbered}
```

Please note that two headings should never directly follow each other in the
text. A heading should always be followed by some text (see, for example, the
beginnings of the chapters here on page \pageref{sec-formal} and
page \pageref{sec-layout}). For further information, see
@sec-list-of-contents.

## Paragraphs

A new paragraph begins after a blank line in the source text. A single line
break in the source text has no effect, so you can -- and should -- start a new
line for each sentence or after about 80 characters. This makes changes easier
to follow in git. The exact appearance of paragraphs in the finished document
is determined by the `parskip` option of the document class -- more on this in
@sec-template.

## Hyphenation {#sec-hyphenation}

The automatic hyphenation in LaTeX works well in principle. However, there
can always be minor problems and undesired results. If you want to influence
the hyphenation for a specific word, add a `\hyphenation{...}` command to
`tex/macros.tex` to specify the permitted hyphenation points. This also allows
you to ensure that certain words are never hyphenated, for example proper names.

For example, words containing a hyphen are *only* separated there, which
can lead to lines not being set correctly, resulting in a warning (see
@sec-compilation). In such cases, you would have to specify additional
hyphenation points manually.

## Enumerations

Markdown provides

* bulleted lists with `*` or `-`,
* numbered lists with `1.`, `2.`, ...,
* definition lists (a term in one line, followed by `: definition`, as at
  the beginning of this chapter).

The exact appearance is set globally for the document.

## Illustrations {#sec-figures}

When someone looks at your finished thesis, it may well be that they first leaf
through it roughly, hardly reading the text but looking at the illustrations.
Hence the "rule" that you should be able to understand the most
important points of the thesis in this way.

Illustrations never stand alone but are described by the *caption*. It
should contain everything that is necessary to understand the illustration.
Only in exceptional cases must the caption refer to the text. Conversely, each
figure must be referenced at least once in the text, see also
@sec-references.

In the following two sections, a distinction is made between images (in
@sec-images) and vector graphics (in @sec-vector-graphics), as these
are completely different techniques that should be used appropriately in each
case.

Remember that not everyone can see all colors equally well. Around 10\ % of
men in Germany, for example, are affected by red-green color-blindness. Your
thesis may also be printed in black and white. Therefore, you should ideally
design illustrations in such a way that they are understandable even without
colors.

### Images {#sec-images}

You include an image with `![Caption](path){#fig-name}`. The identifier
starting with `fig-` makes it a numbered figure that floats to an optimal
position, see @fig-kunst.

![Perhaps this is art?](/images/ThkKunst.png){#fig-kunst width=35%}

```markdown
![Perhaps this is art?](/images/ThkKunst.png){#fig-kunst width=35%}
```

Where a figure may be placed is controlled by `fig-pos` (in this template
`tbh`): `t` stands for the top of the page, `b` for the bottom and `h` for
"here", which means the position within the text. If you need to save space,
`t` and `b` are preferable.

Attention: Many contents such as formulas, code, diagrams, visualization of
data, etc. should not be inserted as an image, but in a suitable form. See the
following section on vector graphics.

### Vector Graphics {#sec-vector-graphics}

You do not need to insert simple illustrations (e.g. coordinate systems,
flowcharts, etc.) as an image. Instead, you can generate them directly in the
source code. The powerful TikZ package is ideal for this: @fig-fleuret is
drawn by `figures/fleuret.tex` from the data in `data/pointsFleuret.csv`.

::: {#fig-fleuret}

```{=latex}
\input{figures/fleuret.tex}
```

A beautiful graphic generated in the source code!
:::

````markdown
::: {#fig-fleuret}
```{=latex}
\input{figures/fleuret.tex}
```

A beautiful graphic generated in the source code!
:::
````

One advantage is that your document remains smaller. Another is that the
illustrations usually look more attractive. This is especially true when
viewing on a screen, as vector graphics can be scaled to any size. You can find
lots of examples of TikZ on the Internet. There is also an up-to-date
book [@kottwitz:tikz].

Alternatively, you can create plots from your data with Python while
rendering, see @sec-marimo.

## Tables {#sec-tables}

Tables are written as *pipe tables*. The caption follows after the table,
introduced by a colon, together with an identifier starting with `tbl-`.

| Heading left | Heading right |
|-------------:|--------------:|
|            1 |          2222 |
|           10 |           222 |
|          100 |            22 |

: A simple table {#tbl-example}

```markdown
| Heading left | Heading right |
|-------------:|--------------:|
|            1 |          2222 |

: A simple table {#tbl-example}
```

The colons in the second line define the alignment of the columns. For more
complex tables (merged cells, colored rows), you can use grid tables or raw
LaTeX, e.g. with the `booktabs` and `tabularx` packages.

## Computations with marimo {#sec-marimo}

If your thesis contains measurements, simulations or other evaluations, you
should not paste their results into the text by hand. Instead, put the Python
code that produces figures and tables directly into the chapter. Quarto runs it
on every render with [marimo](https://marimo.io), a reactive Python notebook,
so text, figures and data cannot get out of sync.

A marimo cell is a code block with the class `.marimo`. A chapter with such
cells needs two entries in its front matter (at the very top of the file, as
in this chapter): `engine: marimo` and the Python packages it uses:

```yaml
---
engine: marimo
pyproject: |
  requires-python = "==3.13.*"
  dependencies = [
    "marimo==0.25.2",
    "matplotlib==3.11.2",
    "pandas==3.1.1",
    "tabulate==0.10.0",
  ]
---
```

The packages are installed automatically into an isolated environment by
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), which you need to install once
(`make check` tells you whether it is there). Pin exact versions (`==`) as
above: computed results in a thesis must be reproducible. The packages these
depend on are frozen by a date, `UV_EXCLUDE_NEWER` in the file `_environment`:
uv uses no release published after it. Move the date forward only on purpose
(`make python-date`), and keep it fixed once you submit. All cells of a chapter form one
marimo app, i.e. a later cell can use the variables of an earlier one. Code
is run in the folder of the project, so paths such as `data/...` start there.
By default, only the output of a cell appears in the PDF; with `#| echo: true`
the code is shown as well, as in the following cells.

The first cell loads the data of @fig-fleuret and defines a small helper
`figure()`. It saves a matplotlib figure as vector PDF and inserts it as a
numbered figure with a caption and the identifier `fig-<label>`:

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: true
import marimo as mo
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

data = pd.read_csv("data/pointsFleuret.csv", names=["x", "y", "z"])

def figure(fig, label, caption, width="70%"):
    Path("_generated").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(f"_generated/{label}.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)
    return mo.md(f"![{caption}](/_generated/{label}.pdf)"
                 f"{{#fig-{label} width={width}}}")
```

The next cell creates @fig-measurements:

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.plot(data.x, data.y, "o", color="#CF1820", label="$y$")
ax.plot(data.x, data.z, "x", color="#AF368C", label="$z$")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
ax.legend()
figure(fig, "measurements", "The data of @fig-fleuret, plotted with matplotlib")
```

A table is created as Markdown text with `mo.md()`; the caption and the
identifier are added by a surrounding div, as for any other content
(@tbl-statistics):

::: {#tbl-statistics}
```{python .marimo}
#| echo: true
stats = data.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]]
mo.md(stats.round(3).to_markdown())
```

Statistics of the measured values
:::

The figures are written to the folder `_generated/`, which is not part of the
repository. Rendering a chapter with marimo cells takes a few seconds longer;
the first render also downloads the packages. For larger evaluations, it is
often more convenient to develop the code in a separate marimo notebook
(`uvx marimo edit --sandbox notebooks/analysis.py`) and to move only the final
plotting and table code into the chapter.

## List of Figures and Tables {#sec-captions}

Quarto creates the list of figures and the list of tables automatically. All
figures and tables with an identifier and a caption appear there
(see @sec-images and @sec-tables).

The caption is used by default for these lists. This text is often too long.
You can therefore specify a shorter version with the attribute `fig-scap`
(for figures) or `tbl-scap` (for tables). See also @sec-ref-figures.

## Equations {#sec-formulas}

One of the greatest strengths of LaTeX is that you have many possibilities to
write down formulas simply and beautifully. You can use LaTeX math directly in
Markdown: inline between single dollar signs, displayed between double dollar
signs, followed by an identifier starting with `eq-`. Here is just a small
example (@eq-gauss):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} i &= {\color{THRed}1} + {\color{blue}2} + \ldots + {\color{blue}(n-1)} + {\color{THRed}n} \\
                 &= {\color{THRed}(1 + n)} + {\color{blue}(2 + (n-1))} + \ldots \\
                 &= \frac{n}{2} \cdot (n+1)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-gauss}

However, simple formulas in the text such as $x \in \mathbb{N}$ are of course
also possible. A common mistake here is that the "math mode" is
forgotten in the text: We are talking about the $x$-value and *not* the
x-value.

The error is just as common the other way round, i.e. text is written in math
mode: $a_{wrong} = 42$, but $a_{\mathit{correct}} = 42$, perhaps also
$a_{\text{correct}} = 42$.

Functions such as $\sin$ are automatically displayed well, as in

$$
\sin \alpha = \left( \frac{a}{c} \right)
$$ {#eq-sine}

The brackets have only been inserted here to demonstrate the corresponding
mechanism: automatic scaling of brackets!

Only equations with an identifier get a number, so number exactly those you
refer to. A reference `@eq-gauss` gives "@eq-gauss"; `-@eq-gauss` gives only
the number in parentheses, e.g. "by -@eq-gauss and -@eq-sine". This is a
customization of the template, see @sec-customizations.

Sometimes you want to use your own "operator" that should look the
same. This is exactly what the `\DeclareMathOperator` command is for,
allowing you to add missing functions such as $\sgn(x)$.

It is advisable to give all mathematical symbols that you use in your work
meaningful names in the source code; the easiest way to do this is with the
`\newcommand` command in `tex/macros.tex`. You can then customize how you want
to display the weight vector $\vecW$ in the entire document or what the
imaginary unit $\ci$ with $\ci^2 = -1$ should look like. Of course, this
assumes that you use the designations consistently. However, this also makes
your source code easier to read!

## Theorems, Definitions and Proofs {#sec-theorems}

Mathematical statements are written as divs whose identifier starts with the
type of the statement. An optional heading inside gives the statement a name.
A proof follows in a div with the class `.proof`; it ends with a box.

::: {#def-triangular}
## Triangular number
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th *triangular number* is
$T_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i$.
:::

::: {#thm-gauss}
## Gauss
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $T_n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Pair the first and the last summand, the second and the second to last, and so
on, as in @eq-gauss. Each of the $\frac{n}{2}$ pairs sums to $n+1$; for odd $n$,
the middle summand is half a pair.
:::

::: {#lem-consecutive}
For every $n \geq 2$, $T_n + T_{n-1} = n^2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @thm-gauss, $T_n + T_{n-1} = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + \frac{(n-1)n}{2} = n^2$.
:::

::: {#cor-integer}
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the product $n(n+1)$ is even.
:::

::: {#prp-cubes}
## Nicomachus
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i^3 = T_n^2$.
:::

::: {#exm-four}
$T_4 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 = \frac{4 \cdot 5}{2}$.
:::

::: {#rem-legend}
According to a well-known anecdote, Gauss found @thm-gauss as a schoolboy.
:::

The source of @def-triangular, @thm-gauss and its proof:

````markdown
::: {#def-triangular}
## Triangular number
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th *triangular number* is
$T_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i$.
:::

::: {#thm-gauss}
## Gauss
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $T_n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Pair the first and the last summand, ...
:::
````

All statements of a chapter share one counter: @def-triangular is followed by
@thm-gauss, @lem-consecutive and so on, which makes each number easy to find
(a customization, see @sec-customizations).
Theorems, lemmas, corollaries and propositions are set in italics;
definitions and examples upright; remarks upright with an italic heading.

| Statement | Identifier | Reference gives |
|-----------|------------|-----------------|
| Definition | `#def-...` | @def-triangular |
| Theorem | `#thm-...` | @thm-gauss |
| Lemma | `#lem-...` | @lem-consecutive |
| Corollary | `#cor-...` | @cor-integer |
| Proposition | `#prp-...` | @prp-cubes |
| Example | `#exm-...` | @exm-four |
| Remark | `#rem-...` | @rem-legend |

: Mathematical statements {#tbl-statements}

Further types are conjecture (`#cnj-`), exercise (`#exr-`) and solution
(`#sol-`). A statement without an identifier, e.g. `::: {.theorem}`, is not
numbered.

## Source Code, Pseudocode {#sec-listing}

If a section of source code is to be displayed in the final thesis, the
obvious idea is to simply take a screenshot of it and display it as an image.
However, this is not a good idea, as the text pixelates when the finished
document is zoomed in. Instead, use a *fenced code block* with the name of the
programming language; Quarto then highlights the syntax automatically. With an
identifier starting with `lst-` and a caption, the code becomes a numbered
listing, see @lst-quicksort.

```{#lst-quicksort .py lst-cap="Quicksort in Python"}
def quicksort(xs):
    if len(xs) <= 1:
        return xs
    pivot, *rest = xs
    smaller = [x for x in rest if x < pivot]
    larger = [x for x in rest if x >= pivot]
    return quicksort(smaller) + [pivot] + quicksort(larger)
```

The source of this listing looks like this:

````markdown
```{#lst-quicksort .py lst-cap="Quicksort in Python"}
def quicksort(xs):
    ...
```
````

The language is given by its name or file extension (`.py`, `.c`, `.java`,
`.rust`, ...). In chapters with marimo cells (@sec-marimo), always write
`.py` for Python listings: a block marked `.python` is treated as a marimo
cell there and stops the render.

The colors are controlled by the option `highlight-style` in `_quarto.yml`.
To show a file from your project, use the include shortcode inside a code
block, e.g. `{{{< include ../src/main.c >}}}`.

*Pseudocode* is written as an algorithm, one of Quarto's statement types: a
div whose identifier starts with `alg-`, with an optional name as heading and
the pseudocode in a raw LaTeX block (@alg-euclid). The commands (`\Procedure`,
`\While`, `\State`, `\Return`, ...) are those of the package `algpseudocodex`.
Algorithms are numbered separately from theorems and are listed in the List of
Algorithms.

::: {#alg-euclid}
## Euclid

```{=latex}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Procedure{Euclid}{$a, b$}
  \While{$b \neq 0$}
    \State $(a, b) \gets (b, a \bmod b)$
  \EndWhile
  \State \Return $a$
\EndProcedure
\end{algorithmic}
```
:::

````markdown
::: {#alg-euclid}
## Euclid

```{=latex}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Procedure{Euclid}{$a, b$}
  \While{$b \neq 0$}
    \State $(a, b) \gets (b, a \bmod b)$
  \EndWhile
  \State \Return $a$
\EndProcedure
\end{algorithmic}
```
:::
````

## Further Directories {#sec-glossaries}

Additional directories are created using the LaTeX `glossaries` package. A
glossary and lists of abbreviations and symbols are already set up. All entries
are defined in the file `tex/glossary.tex`; only entries that are actually
used in the text appear in the lists. The lists are inserted after the table
of contents and listed there. Which lists are printed is set in the
`thesis: lists:` block of `_quarto.yml`.

The template uses the `\makenoidxglossaries` mode of the package, so no
external program is needed to sort the entries.

### Creating a Glossary

An entry in the glossary is defined in `tex/glossary.tex`:

```latex
\newglossaryentry{dog}{name={Dog}, description={Hairy, four-legged mammal}}
```

The term is then displayed in the text with `\gls{dog}`. Want an example? The
\gls{dog} is man's best friend.

### Creating a List of Abbreviations

An abbreviation is defined in `tex/glossary.tex` with the label, the
abbreviation and the long form:

```latex
\newacronym{svm}{SVM}{support vector machine}
```

It is then used in the text with `\gls{svm}`. LaTeX automatically ensures that
the abbreviation is written out the first time it is mentioned in the text. For all subsequent
mentions, only the abbreviation is then displayed. Want an example? This is a
\gls{svm}. And here is another \gls{svm}. Use `\glspl{svm}` for the plural.

### Creating a List of Symbols

A symbol is defined like a glossary entry, but with the additional key
`type=symbols`. The command `\gls{label}` can then be used to display the
symbol in the text -- also in formulas. Need an example? The force
\gls{sym:force} is defined according to the following equation:

$$
\gls{sym:force} = m \cdot \vec{a}
$$

## References {#sec-references}

Everything numbered gets an identifier; `@identifier` in the text then gives
the name and the number, and the PDF links to it. @tbl-references lists all
numbered elements of this template.

| Element | Identifier | Example | Reference gives |
|---------|------------|---------|-----------------|
| Chapter, section | `{#sec-...}` | @sec-headings | @sec-headings |
| Figure | `{#fig-...}` | @sec-images | @fig-kunst |
| Table | `{#tbl-...}` | @sec-tables | @tbl-example |
| Equation | `{#eq-...}` | @sec-formulas | @eq-gauss |
| Statement (theorem, ...) | `#thm-...` etc. | @sec-theorems | @thm-gauss |
| Listing | `#lst-...` | @sec-listing | @lst-quicksort |
| Algorithm | `#alg-...` | @sec-listing | @alg-euclid |

: Numbered elements and their references {#tbl-references}

Sections, figures, tables, listings, equations and algorithms each have their
own counter; all mathematical statements share one. If you only want the number,
write `-@fig-kunst` (-@fig-kunst); for the page, use `\pageref{fig-kunst}`
(page \pageref{fig-kunst}). Several references at once: `[@thm-gauss;
@lem-consecutive]` gives [@thm-gauss; @lem-consecutive].

Every figure and every table must be referenced in the text; no numbered
environments may simply "hang in the air". In contrast, sections and equations
do not all have to be explicitly referenced. However, you can help your readers
by thinking about meaningful references.

## Special Spaces and Signs {#sec-special-cases}

A line break (or even a page break) can always occur at spaces. This should be
avoided in some cases, partly because lines should not start with numbers. A
typical example is "Figure\ 3". Here you need a so-called protected
space after "Figure", which is created in Markdown with a backslash followed
by a space (`Figure\ 3`). Cross-references such as `@fig-kunst` get one
automatically.

Horizontal spacing between words and sentences is dynamically adjusted in each
line. This template uses `\frenchspacing`, so the space after the dot in
abbreviations such as "e.g." is not too large.

As with spaces, there are also different lengths for horizontal dashes. For
dashes -- here, for example -- or if "to" is meant (as in 14:00--16:00), the
single hyphen (minus sign) is not sufficient, the appropriate dash is created
by a double minus (`--`).

Only a few characters have a special function in Markdown, e.g. `*`, `_`, `#`,
`$`, `@`, `[` and `]`, as well as `<` and `\`. If you want to output them
literally, put a backslash in front of them: `\$` gives \$, `\@` gives \@.
Characters such as % and & that are problematic in LaTeX can be typed
directly.

Quotation marks are set automatically in the correct style of the document
language when you type straight quotes ("..." or '...').

## Selecting the Basic Font

By default, LaTeX uses a serif font (Latin Modern) for continuous text. Serif
fonts are advantageous for printed work because the serifs emphasize the
baseline and thus help the eye to jump back to the beginning of the next line
at the end of the line. In addition, the different stroke widths lead to
clearer word images and thus support the reading process.

However, if such a document is viewed on an old monitor with a low resolution,
the fine serifs may no longer be displayed properly. In such a case, it may be
advantageous to use a sans serif font. It may also be that sans serif fonts are
preferred for reasons of accessibility.

As this template uses `lualatex`, you can use any font installed on your
computer. Add the following to the `thk-thesis-pdf` format in
`_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
format:
  thk-thesis-pdf:
    mainfont: "Arial"     # or e.g. "TeX Gyre Pagella", "Source Serif 4"
    sansfont: "Arial"
```

## Metadata for the PDF Viewer

Some PDF viewers can display additional metadata, such as the name of the
author, the title of the document (also different from the name of the file) or
keywords. This template takes them from `book: title`, `book: author` and
`keywords` in `_quarto.yml`.

In addition, links in the document can be highlighted as colored text.
For a printed thesis this is usually not wanted, so it is switched off. If
you prefer colored links on screen, set `colorlinks: true` in the format
options.

## Switch Between Single and Double-sided Layout

This template is optimized for a one-sided layout. The left and right margins
are the same size on all pages and new chapters start immediately on the next
page. When the finished PDF document is viewed on the computer, it looks just
right. However, if the document is to be printed double-sided, the layout can
be adjusted slightly. Typically, the inner margins are then slightly narrower
than the outer margins. New chapters always start on a new, right-hand
page -- which can lead to individual blank pages between the chapters. This
looks better for double-sided documents.

To activate the double-sided layout, add the following lines to the
`thk-thesis-pdf` format in `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
    classoption: [BCOR=8mm, headings=normal, parskip=half, headsepline,
                  automark, listof=totoc, bibliography=totoc,
                  twoside, open=right]
```

## Compile {#sec-compilation}

You create the PDF with `make` (or `quarto render`) in the folder of your
thesis; it ends up in `_book/thesis.pdf`. During writing, `make preview` (or
`quarto preview`) is more convenient: the PDF is updated every time you save a
file. Your editor (VS Code, Positron, RStudio) has buttons for both. `make help`
lists all available commands.

Rendering a large document takes some time. As you usually work on only a few
chapters at a time, you can comment out the remaining chapters in
`_quarto.yml` with `#`.

Basically, the aim should be for your document to compile without warnings. The
best thing to do is to regularly take care of rectifying any problems.

A typical warning is about an unresolved cross-reference or citation, shown as
`?@fig-xyz` in the PDF. In this case, check the identifier for typos.

Boxes that are too full (a line sticks out into the margin) or too empty (a
line with large gaps) are listed by `make warnings`: it renders the thesis,
keeps the LaTeX log and shows each warning with the matching lines of the
generated `thesis.tex`, so you can find the place in your text. To avoid lines that are too
long, it sometimes helps to mark hyphenation points (see @sec-hyphenation).
Otherwise, a sentence may have to be minimally reworded.

Every push to the repository on GitHub also renders the thesis automatically;
the PDF can be downloaded from the *Actions* tab. Your supervisor therefore
always sees the current state.

## This Template {#sec-template}

The layout is defined by the Quarto extension in `_extensions/thk-thesis/`. It
uses KOMA-Script[^koma], a "collection of classes and packages for LaTeX",
with carefully chosen typographic defaults. Please do not change the files in
the extension; your own LaTeX commands belong in `tex/macros.tex`, your glossary
entries in `tex/glossary.tex`. Improvements of the template can then be
installed with `make update-template`.

The document class options (`classoption` in the extension) determine, among
other things, the font size, the binding correction (`BCOR`), the size of the
headings (`headings`) and the spacing between paragraphs (`parskip`). In
principle, you can also influence the size of the margins with the `DIV`
option, but this is not recommended. The margins are automatically set so that
lines have a length that is easy to read.

The header shows the current chapter heading at the top right of the page; the
page number is at the bottom right. The most important packages are:

`babel`
: Selects English (from `lang` in `_quarto.yml`) and its hyphenation patterns.

`selnolig`
: Ensures that ligatures are set correctly (with `lualatex`).

`microtype`
: Optimizes the appearance of the text (type area).

`csquotes`
: Typesets quotation marks correctly.

`tikz` and `pgfplots`
: Generate images directly in the source code, see @sec-vector-graphics.

`hyperref`
: Clickable links and bookmarks in the PDF.

`fvextra`
: Wraps long lines in code blocks instead of letting them run into the margin.

`biblatex`
: Citations and bibliography, processed with `biber`, see @sec-literature.

`amsmath`, `amssymb` and `mathtools`
: Great expansion of the possibilities for displaying mathematical content.

`glossaries`
: Glossary, list of abbreviations and list of symbols, see @sec-glossaries.

`amsthm` and `algpseudocodex`
: Theorems, definitions and proofs (@sec-theorems); pseudocode in algorithms
  (@sec-listing).

### Differences from Quarto's Defaults {#sec-customizations}

Everything in this template is standard Quarto, except for a few
customizations in the extension `_extensions/thk-thesis/`. If you read
Quarto's documentation, these are the places where the template behaves
differently:

Shared counter for statements
: Quarto numbers each type of statement separately (Definition 3.1,
  Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.1). Here, all statements of a chapter share one
  counter (Definition 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Lemma 3.3), see @sec-theorems.
  Algorithms keep their own counter.

Equation references
: Quarto refers to an equation numbered (3.1) as "Equation 3.1". Here,
  `@eq-...` gives "Equation (3.1)" and `-@eq-...` gives "(3.1)", matching the
  number next to the equation.

List of Algorithms
: Algorithms (`#alg-...`) are typeset as in Quarto, but are also collected in
  a List of Algorithms after the table of contents.

Front matter and back matter
: Cover page, abstract, the lists after the abstract (table of contents,
  figures, tables, listings, algorithms, glossary, abbreviations, symbols)
  with Roman page numbers, the position of the bibliography before the
  appendix, and the declaration are generated from the `thesis:` block in
  `_quarto.yml`.

Layout
: KOMA-Script class `scrreprt` with header and page numbers as in the TH Köln
  LaTeX template, biblatex instead of Quarto's default bibliography processing,
  and code blocks that wrap long lines. The titles "Contents" and "Appendix"
  (Quarto: "Table of contents", "Appendices") are set under `language:` in
  `_quarto.yml`.

The template's own Lua filter (`thk-thesis.lua`) and LaTeX files
(`thk-header.tex`, `partials/`) contain all of this; their comments mark each
customization.

[^koma]: <https://komascript.de>
